summary: An Applicability Statement describing how to exchange structured business data, such as XML or EDI, securely using FTP with MIME packaging. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4823 defines Applicability Statement 3 (AS3) for exchanging Electronic Data Interchange (EDI), XML and other documents over File Transfer Protocol (FTP). Messages use Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) and Secure MIME (S/MIME) for signatures, encryption and receipts.

subtitle: A method for exchanging signed or encrypted business documents over FTP.

tldr.problem: Businesses exchanging EDI, XML or other structured data over FTP need options for confidentiality, integrity, authentication and receipts.
tldr.mechanism: AS3 packages data as a MIME message, applies S/MIME signatures or encryption as agreed, sends it using FTP and returns a Message Disposition Notification when requested.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4823 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8996 according to the supplied metadata.

today: RFC 4823 is an Informational RFC published in April 2007 and has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: What AS3 Defines
sections.content:
AS3 is an applicability statement for exchanging structured business data over FTP. It covers EDI, XML, binary data and other content that can be packaged using standard MIME content types.

The message can be signed, encrypted or sent without those protections, depending on the trading partners' chosen process. The receiver can poll an FTP server, process an incoming message and return a message disposition acknowledgement.
sections.plainLanguage: This method sets out how trading partners can exchange business data through FTP. Partners choose whether messages are signed, encrypted and acknowledged.

sections.title: The Secure Transmission Loop
sections.content:
The Secure Transmission Loop is a two-step option: the sender sends a signed and encrypted document requesting a signed receipt, and the receiver decrypts the document, checks its signature and returns a signed receipt.

The receipt is a Message Disposition Notification (MDN). For non-repudiation of receipt as defined by the RFC, the sender must verify the signed receipt; the specification does not require every trading relationship to use the loop.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can request a signed receipt for a signed and encrypted message. The receiver checks it and returns a signed notification, which the sender must verify.

sections.title: MIME Messages and AS3 Headers
sections.content:
An AS3 message is a MIME message with ordinary MIME headers and AS3-specific outer headers. Required headers include AS3-To, AS3-From, Date, Message-ID and Content-Type; sender and recipient names are case-sensitive and contain 1 to 128 printable ASCII characters.

A message requesting a receipt must include Disposition-Notification-To. A signed receipt request also specifies a signature protocol and message-integrity-check algorithm; a message ID is limited to 998 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message identifies its sender and recipient and includes a message ID. A receipt request adds a header telling the receiver where to return its notification.

sections.title: FTP Delivery and MDN Receipts
sections.content:
AS3 requires FTP clients and servers to support the AUTH command, and AUTH TLS support is mandatory. The sender uploads a message; the receiver returns an MDN over a separate FTP connection.

A signed MDN contains a multipart report and a signature. Its Received-content-MIC field carries a digest of the received content so the sender can compare it with a locally calculated digest.
sections.plainLanguage: The message and its receipt use separate FTP connections. A signed receipt includes a digest of the received content for the sender to check.

sections.title: Certificates and Security
sections.content:
Trading partners establish their public-key exchange as part of setting up their relationship. X.509 certificates are required, but using a certification authority is optional; partners are recommended to certify each other's keys when they have no agreed authority.

The complete certificate chain must be included and verification must chain to a root. If a certificate cannot be shown to be valid, for example because it expired or was revoked, the software should clearly notify the user. The RFC also says 40-bit encryption is weak.
sections.plainLanguage: Trading partners need to exchange and check certificates before sending protected messages. Software should clearly report certificate problems, and the RFC warns that 40-bit encryption is weak.
